title: Cap. VIII Arg.: if God reprobates from himself, fewer reprobates than predestined (Ps. 145:9; Gregory of Valencia)
pass_a_gloss: So some argue: If God were to reprobate men not on account of the sins of men, but of his own accord and from himself, then there would be fewer reprobated than predestined. For God is far more inclined from himself unto having mercy and doing good unto men, than unto deserting, destroying, and damning them, according to that of the Psalm, Psalm 145:9. The Lord is sweet unto all, and his compassions are over all his works. This reason Gregory of Valencia (from whom we have taken most of the superior arguments) pronounces in his judgment to be the best, and professes that it was borrowed by him from John Fekius.
pass_b_english: Some argue thus: if God reprobated men not for their sins, but of his own accord and from himself, then there would be fewer reprobate than predestined. For God is far more inclined from himself to mercy and beneficence than to deserting, destroying, and damning — according to Psalm 145:9: The Lord is sweet to all, and his compassions are over all his works. Gregory of Valencia (from whom we have taken most of the earlier arguments) judges this the best reason, and says he borrowed it from John Fekius.
source_text: Sic argutantur quidam: Si Deus non propter peccata hominum, sed sua sponte et ex seipso, homines reprobaret, tum pauciores essent reprobati quam praedestinati. Nam Deus longe propensior est ex se ad miserendum et benefaciendum hominibus, quam ad deserendos, perdendos, et damnandos, juxta illud Psalmi, Psal. cxlv. 9. Suavis Dominus universis, et miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus. Hanc rationem Gregorius de Valentia (ex quo pleraque superiora argumenta desumpsimus) suo judicio optimam esse pronunciat, eamque se a Joanne Fekio mutuatam fuisse profitetur.
